A pagan is a person whose religious or spiritual beliefs fall outside the three major Abrahamic faiths — Christianity, Judaism, and Islam. These three religions are called "Abrahamic" because they all trace their roots to the prophet Abraham and worship a single God. Anyone who does not belong to one of these three has historically been called a pagan.

That is the broadest definition. In everyday use today, however, the word most commonly refers to someone who follows an earth-centered, nature-based, or polytheistic (many-gods) spiritual tradition — either an ancient one or a modern revival of such traditions.

While there is no single pagan rulebook, most pagans share some common threads.

Many gods, not one. Most pagan traditions are polytheistic, meaning they believe in multiple gods and goddesses, each representing a different force of nature or aspect of life. The ancient Greeks believed in Zeus (sky and thunder), Athena (wisdom), Poseidon (the sea), and many others. The Norse people believed in Odin (wisdom and war), Thor (thunder), and Freya (love and fertility). This is fundamentally different from Abrahamic religions, which teach that there is only one God.

Deep reverence for nature. Pagans typically see the natural world — the sun, the moon, the seasons, rivers, forests, and animals — as sacred. Their spiritual practices and festivals are often tied to the rhythms of nature, such as the summer solstice (the longest day of the year), the winter solstice (the shortest), and the changing of seasons. Nature is not just a backdrop; it is the stage on which their spirituality plays out.

No single holy scripture. Unlike Christianity, which has the Bible, Islam, which has the Quran, or Judaism, which has the Torah, most pagan traditions do not have one central sacred text that all followers must read and obey. Knowledge is passed down through oral tradition, ritual, and community practice.

No central authority. There is no "pagan pope," no single church, and no single headquarters. Different pagan traditions are independent of each other, and even within a tradition, individuals often have a lot of freedom in how they practice.

A personal, lived spirituality. Paganism tends to be highly experiential — meaning it is about what you do and feel, not just what you believe intellectually. Rituals, ceremonies, dances, offerings to gods, working with herbs and the land — these are as important as doctrines.

The word was used — often as a weapon — by early Christians to describe anyone who was not Christian. It carried a heavy negative connotation, essentially meaning "uncivilized," "ungodly," or "belonging to the darkness." Romans, Greeks, Celts, Egyptians, Norse people — all were painted with this brush by the early Church.

As Christianity spread across Europe over many centuries, pagan beliefs were actively suppressed. Temples to the old gods were torn down or converted into churches. Ancient festivals were banned or absorbed into Christian holidays (Christmas, for instance, was partly placed in late December to coincide with existing pagan winter festivals). People were pressured — and sometimes violently forced — to abandon their traditions and convert. This is why so many ancient pagan traditions were lost or survived only in fragments.

To make this concrete, here are some of the most famous pagan religious traditions in history. The ancient Greek religion worshipped a large family of gods on Mount Olympus and is the source of the myths about Hercules, Medusa, and the Trojan War. The Roman religion was very similar, essentially adopting the Greek gods and giving them Latin names — Zeus became Jupiter, Ares became Mars, Aphrodite became Venus. The Norse religion, followed by the Vikings and other Germanic peoples of Scandinavia, gave us Odin, Thor, and the concept of Valhalla. The Celtic religion, practiced across ancient Britain, Ireland, and Gaul (modern France), is associated with the mysterious priestly class known as the Druids. The ancient Egyptian religion, one of the oldest in the world, featured gods like Ra (the sun god), Osiris (the god of death and resurrection), and Anubis (the jackal-headed god of the afterlife).

What all of these share is polytheism, rich mythology, and a deep connection between the divine and the forces of the natural world.

Today, many people actively and proudly identify as pagans. This modern movement is often called neo-paganism, meaning "new paganism." These are people who have either revived ancient traditions, reconstructed them from historical records, or created new spiritual paths inspired by them.

Wicca is perhaps the most well-known modern pagan tradition. It was developed in the mid-20th century and centers on the worship of a god and a goddess, the casting of spells, and the celebration of eight seasonal festivals called "Sabbats." Wiccans often describe their core ethical principle as: "Do what you will, as long as it harms none."

Druidry is a modern spiritual path inspired by the ancient Celtic Druids. It emphasizes connection to nature, creativity, wisdom, and community, often through ceremony conducted outdoors.

Heathenry (also called Asatru) is a reconstruction of the pre-Christian Norse and Germanic religion — the religion of the Vikings. Practitioners honor gods like Odin and Thor through offerings, feasts, and community rituals.

Hellenism is the revival of the ancient Greek religion — people today who genuinely worship Zeus, Athena, and the rest of the Olympian pantheon.

These are just a few examples. The modern pagan world is diverse and decentralized, with many overlapping traditions.
What Paganism is NOT — Clearing Up Misconceptions

This is critically important because the word "pagan" comes loaded with historical misunderstanding.

Pagans are not Satanists. This is perhaps the biggest and most harmful misconception. Satan — the Devil — is a concept that comes entirely from Christianity and Islam. The old pagan religions had no Satan. Worshipping Thor or Aphrodite or celebrating the winter solstice has absolutely nothing to do with devil worship. The confusion arose partly because the Christian Church, when trying to discredit pagan traditions, depicted pagan gods as demonic. The pointed ears and hooved feet we associate with the Devil were actually borrowed from Pan, the playful Greek god of the wilderness.

Pagan does not mean evil or immoral. Historically the word was used as an insult, but pagan traditions often contain rich ethical and philosophical frameworks about living in harmony with nature, treating one's community with honor, and respecting the forces of the universe.

Pagan does not mean primitive or uneducated. The ancient Greeks — often labeled pagans by Christians — built one of the most philosophically, artistically, and scientifically advanced civilizations in history. Plato, Aristotle, Socrates, Pythagoras — all were pagans. Their thought still shapes the modern world. Calling something "pagan" has never meant it was intellectually or morally inferior.
The Tone of the Word — Does It Sound Like an Insult?

The short answer: it depends entirely on context.

In an academic or historical setting, "pagan" is a neutral, descriptive term — a scholar using it simply means "a follower of a non-Abrahamic, typically polytheistic religion." There is no insult intended, and none should be inferred.

In traditional religious contexts — particularly conservative Christianity — the word may still carry a negative charge, used to describe someone as ungodly or spiritually lost.

Among modern pagans themselves, the word is a source of pride and identity. Calling yourself a pagan today is an act of self-definition, not shame.

So the word itself is neither inherently good nor bad — it is a label whose emotional weight shifts depending on who is using it and why.

A pagan is someone who follows a spiritual or religious tradition that sits outside Christianity, Judaism, and Islam — most often a polytheistic (many-gods) or nature-based tradition. Historically, the word was used by Christians as a dismissive label for those who worshipped the old gods of Greece, Rome, Scandinavia, Egypt, and the Celtic world. Over centuries, many of these traditions were suppressed or lost. Today, the word has been reclaimed positively by a growing number of people — Wiccans, Druids, Heathens, Hellenists, and others — who follow modern revivals of these ancient spiritual paths. A pagan is not a Satanist, not a devil worshipper, and not someone without ethics — those are myths. A pagan is simply someone walking a spiritual road that is older than, and distinct from, the Abrahamic faiths.
